title: why it's said three times
hook: om shanti shanti shanti: three times, never once, and there's a reason
tomorrow: why Indian kids touch their grandparents' feet

segments.voice: Yesterday, dharma: what holds things up. Your line was do the thing that's yours to do. Did you do one piece of the frozen thing? If not, it's still there, and that's fine. Day four.

Om shanti shanti shanti. It closes the peace chants that open the Upanishads, and you may have heard it at the end of a class or a ceremony. Count them. Not once. Not twice. Three times. Repeating a word for emphasis is common enough, but there's a more specific answer here. Traditional teachers explain the three shantis as a kind of checklist, a diagnosis of where trouble comes from. And the three make a handy way to sort an ordinary day.

Shanti means peace. Not the peace of a treaty. The settled kind: calm, quiet, water with nothing stirring it. The Bhagavad Gita asks a blunt question about it. For someone without peace, it says, how can there be happiness? Now, the three. An old philosophical text, the Samkhya Karika, begins by naming suffering of three kinds. And some teachers read the three shantis against that list. Peace from trouble that comes from forces beyond anyone's control, which the old commentators tie to the gods and the elements: storms, floods, the weather, the world. Peace from trouble that comes from other beings: the text that stung, the friend who didn't call, the driver who cut in. And peace from trouble that comes from within: your own body and your own mind. An aching back. The replay that won't switch off. The sentence said years ago that nobody else remembers. The world. Other people. Yourself. Three sources, three shantis. Some teachers who use this list point out something practical. There's only a little anyone can do about the first. There's somewhat more to do about the second. The third is the one most within reach, and it's also the easiest one to skip. So when a prayer or a reading ends this way, it isn't padding. It's going down the list. Peace out there. Peace between us. Peace in here. And then it stops. There's nothing to add after the third one.
screen: `1 — THE WORLD.` · `2 — OTHER PEOPLE.` · `3 — YOUR OWN MIND.` · `THE THIRD IS WITHIN REACH.` · then, large: `THREE SOURCES. THREE PEACES.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell, one shanti on each. First breath out: shanti, toward the world, whatever's on fire out there today. Second breath out: shanti, toward one person you're not at peace with. You don't have to forgive them. Just wish the space between you quieter. Third breath out: shanti, toward your own mind. As kindly as you'd say it to a friend.
Shanti. Peace, the settled kind. Said three times, for three directions: the world, others, and your own mind. Fourth word.
Your line: peace, peace, peace. When something rattles you today, notice which of the three it came from: the world, another person, or your own mind. Just notice. That's day four.

howItsDone: Hindu prayers, readings of the Upanishads and ceremonies often close with om shanti shanti shanti, the word for peace said three times.

myth: shanti is said three times just for the rhythm
traditional teachers read the three as three sources of trouble: the world, others, and yourself.
the Gita asks how someone without peace can be happy
Bhagavad Gita 2.66: without peace, how can there be happiness?

fork.setup: someone cuts you off in traffic. then you replay it in your head for the next hour. which shanti does the hour of replay need?
fork.reveal: the driver was other people. the hour of replay is the third, your own mind, the one that's most within reach.

original.note: Sanskrit: peace, calm, quiet. said three times at the close of the peace chants.

trapdoor: what you thought: a calm word to end on.
what it means: peace in three directions: the world, other people, your own mind.
what a scholar hears: the Samkhya Karika opens with threefold suffering; commentators name it from within (adhyatmika), from other beings (adhibhautika) and from forces beyond (adhidaivika).

sources.ref: shanti patha (the peace chants of the Upanishads, e.g. the invocation of the Isha Upanishad)

notes: Samkhya Karika 1 names threefold suffering (duhkha-traya); the division into adhyatmika, adhibhautika and adhidaivika comes from the commentaries (e.g. Gaudapada). The script says 'some teachers read the three shantis against that list'; confirm the attribution and that the pairing with the three shantis is a fair traditional reading.

Hook says om shanti shanti shanti 'closes the peace chants that open the Upanishads'; confirm phrasing (the shanti patha attached to the principal Upanishads). 'Some of the oldest Hindu texts' was cut as a superlative.

Cut from manuscript day 4 under the claims rule: 'the ancient texts, which are otherwise extremely economical with words', 'one of the most practical ideas in the whole tradition', 'the thing you said in 2019', and 'the ending of every prayer, every class, every text'.
Audit pass: adhidaivika is literally trouble from the devas; the teach now says the commentators tie it to the gods and the elements, so 'forces beyond anyone's control' is not a bare modern gloss.

Editor pass: 'illness' moved out of the first shanti (bodily illness belongs to adhyatmika, trouble from within, in the commentaries) and replaced with storms and floods; 'an aching back' added to the third; 'the replay at two in the morning' trimmed (late-night image echoed day 1) and 'the sentence you said' made impersonal; 'you'll start sorting your own day' (predicting the listener) softened; the within-reach point now attributed to teachers who use the list.
